passages.title: Optical Character Recognition in Historical Polytonic Texts
passages.body: Digitizing dusty nineteenth-century newspapers once promised instant searchable history, yet humanities researchers soon encountered garbled optical-character-recognition (OCR) transcripts riddled with 'rn' mistyped for 'm' or fading ink blots turning numerals into random symbols. Standard office OCR engines trained on crisp laser-printed English novels struggle acutely when parsing irregular movable lead type pressed onto acidic yellowish newsprint or ancient multilingual classics carrying overlapping diacritics and ligatures. Recent digital-humanities pipelines deploy neural sequence models paired carefully with custom typography data-augmentation—deliberately simulating ink bleed, slight skewed baselines, and foxing stains across clean fonts—trimming error rates sharply down below two percent on multi-column gazettes. Even so, project archivists stress transparent raw scan preservation alongside plain-text correction logs so future scholars can audit tricky historical proper nouns back straight against original page pixels.

passages.title: Tree Canopies and Urban Particulate Air Scrubbing
passages.body: Street-level urban air monitors often record sharp particulate PM2.5 spikes directly downwind of jammed morning diesel expressways, yet air samples collected merely thirty meters inward behind dense leafy conifer hedges frequently show thirty percent drops in ultrafine soot burdens. Rather than passively blocking particles like flat concrete walls—which simply deflect air eddies abruptly upward over backyards—complex rough evergreen needle clusters and fine fuzzy trichome hairs along broadleaf undersides trap heavy airborne particulates electrostatically and mechanically until summer rainfall rinses heavy metals safely downward toward soil microbes. Equally nuanced, urban canyon geometry matters acutely: tightly packed giant tree canopies above narrow sluggish four-lane streets surrounded by tall brick towers can inadvertently trap exhaust fumes cleanly at sidewalk nose height when cross-breezes vanish—prompting modern planners to tune spacing toward permeable staggered shrub belts along busy avenues.

passages.title: Acoustic Design Inside Historic Wooden Mosque & Church Chambers
passages.body: Before electronic public-address amplifiers arrived in historic stone and timber houses of worship, master builders had to ensure clear spoken sermons carried naturally across crowded galleries without muddying choral chants. In sixteenth-century stone vaults topped by soaring masonry domes, long booming echoes often muddled spoken consonants over three seconds—forcing medieval chanters to slow syllables deliberately while leaving fast ordinary speech nearly incomprehensible across rear bays. Remarkably, several Renaissance and Ottoman sanctuaries solved that clash passively by tucking hundreds of tuned open-necked terracotta acoustic jars ('Helmholtz resonators') horizontally inside mortar arches or upper dome masonry. Each hollow clay vessel vibrated empathetically against narrow booming bass resonance peaks inside the chamber—draining muddy low-frequency droning cleanly out of air without dulling luminous choir harmonies.
